passage:
Mentor's note: Mohit, 25, junior architect
In Tuesday's review, a client said, "This looks like a child did it." Mohit went white. Afterwards he asked me for ten minutes. He said the phrase was exactly what his father used to say about his drawings, and it had hit him as if he were twelve again.
He didn't pretend it was nothing. He cried a little, then wrote down what he remembered in his notebook while I sat nearby. He said this has been coming back a lot, so he has booked a session with a counsellor through the office scheme.
I told him I respected how he handled it. Next: I'll share client feedback with him in writing first, then we'll discuss it.
— Sudha

qa.q: What did the client say about the work?
qa.a: "This looks like a child did it."

qa.q: Why did the client's words hit Mohit so hard?
qa.a: It was exactly what his father used to say about his drawings, so an old hurt came rushing back as if he were twelve again.

qa.q: Which of Mohit's choices helped the old hurt settle?
qa.a: Instead of pushing it down, he talked to Sudha, cried, wrote it down, and booked a counsellor because the feeling keeps coming back.

qa.q: How might Sudha's respect affect Mohit?
qa.a: Hearing that his mentor respected how he handled it may help Mohit feel less ashamed of crying at work, and more willing to keep facing it.

grounding: A mentor's note shows a young architect meeting an old hurt by talking, crying and writing, and booking a counsellor as it keeps recurring.

passage:
Thursday, 10:40 pm
The old hurt came back today, out of nowhere. Someone posted our Class 8 photo in the school group, and there I was in the corner, the year everyone called me "the smell" and nobody sat with me at lunch.
My usual trick is to shut the laptop and scrub the whole kitchen. Tonight I didn't. I sat on the floor and cried properly about it for the first time, I think, ever.
Then I called Maria. She didn't say "That was ages ago." She said, "That sounds so lonely." I cried again, but lighter.
If it keeps coming back like this, I'll ask about the counselling service at work. For now: writing, water, sleep.
— Dilnaz

qa.q: What was posted in the school group?
qa.a: The Class 8 photo.

qa.q: Why did Dilnaz cry 'lighter' after talking to Maria?
qa.a: Maria named the loneliness instead of brushing it off, so Dilnaz felt understood and some of the old weight lifted.

qa.q: What choice did Dilnaz make instead of the usual trick?
qa.a: Rather than shutting the laptop and scrubbing the kitchen, Dilnaz let the tears come, called a trusted friend and wrote it down, with counselling as the next step if it keeps returning.

qa.q: What might Maria have felt hearing about the Class 8 year?
qa.a: Maria was probably sad for the younger Dilnaz and glad to be trusted with it 🤍

grounding: A young adult's diary shows an old school hurt met with tears, a call to a trusted friend and writing, with counselling in mind if it persists.

passage: After school in the kasba near Hoshangabad, Vishal, twenty-four, sat alone in the empty staffroom, hands shaking. In class, a boy had frozen at the blackboard and another had jeered, "Useless, just like his father." Vishal had stopped it at once. But the words had hit him too: his own father used to say them. He had thought that was long behind him. His first urge was to shove it down and mark copies. Instead he opened his diary and wrote exactly what he felt, even the angry part. That evening he told his wife, Usha, on the terrace. His voice cracked, and he cried, and she held his hand. "If this keeps coming back and weighs on you," she said, "let's find a counsellor together." Vishal nodded. The next morning, he took the jeering student aside, and then the frozen one.

qa.q: What did the student jeer at the boy at the blackboard?
qa.a: "Useless, just like his father."

qa.q: Why did the jeer hit Vishal so hard?
qa.a: It echoed words his own father used to say to him, bringing back an old hurt he thought was long behind him.

qa.q: What did Vishal choose instead of shoving the feeling down?
qa.a: He wrote exactly what he felt in his diary and later told Usha, letting himself cry, and they agreed to find a counsellor if it kept weighing on him.

qa.q: How might Usha have felt listening to Vishal on the terrace?
qa.a: She seemed caring and steady, holding his hand and offering to look for a counsellor together.

grounding: A young teacher lets an old hurt be spoken by writing and talking to his wife instead of pushing it down, with a counsellor as a possible ally.

passage: At his cousin's wedding in Seville, Alejandro, twenty-six, watched the bride dance with her father, and something old cracked open. His own father had left when he was ten and never came to his graduation. He'd told himself for years that it didn't matter. Now his throat locked and he walked out to the car park. His first instinct was to go back in, smile, and have another drink. Instead he called Zanele, his closest friend from university. "It's stupid," he said. "It was sixteen years ago." "It's not stupid," Zanele said. "Tell me." He talked for twenty minutes and cried twice. Afterward he felt emptied, but lighter. Over the next month the feeling kept coming back at odd moments, so he booked an appointment with a counsellor at the clinic near work. "Good," Zanele texted. "I'm proud of you."

qa.q: How old was Alejandro when his father left?
qa.a: He was ten.

qa.q: Why did Alejandro say "It's stupid" on the phone?
qa.a: Part of him still felt he shouldn't be hurting after sixteen years, as if the old pain didn't deserve attention.

qa.q: Which choices did Alejandro make instead of shoving the feeling down?
qa.a: He called a trusted friend and let himself talk and cry, and when the feeling kept returning, he booked a counsellor.

qa.q: How might Zanele feel hearing Alejandro finally talk about his father?
qa.a: Zanele seemed warm and glad he reached out, and proud of him for booking the counsellor.

grounding: A young man lets an old hurt be spoken with a trusted friend instead of pushing it down, then seeks a counsellor when it persists.

passage: At the Pune office, the communication workshop included a role-play where one person had to mock another's work. Ujjwal played the one being mocked. Halfway through, his throat closed and his hands shook; he was suddenly thirteen, in the school corridor, with the same laughter around him. He'd buried that year deep. He asked to step out. In the stairwell, instead of washing his face and pretending, he did something new: he messaged his team lead, Hemant. "The role-play hit an old nerve. I need ten minutes." Hemant came out. Ujjwal told him, briefly, about school. His voice cracked, and he let it. Hemant listened. "Thank you for telling me. The company has a counsellor. Want me to help you book a session?" Ujjwal nodded. He booked it that afternoon.

qa.q: What did the role-play ask one person to do?
qa.a: Mock another's work.

qa.q: Why did Ujjwal's hands shake during the role-play?
qa.a: The mocking brought back buried memories of being laughed at in school, so he was suddenly flooded with old hurt and fear.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal do differently this time, and why does it matter?
qa.a: He told his team lead instead of pretending, and booked a counsellor, letting the old hurt be spoken and supported rather than buried.

qa.q: How might Hemant see Ujjwal's message?
qa.a: Hemant likely felt concerned but respected that Ujjwal trusted him, and responded supportively by listening and offering the counsellor.

grounding: Shows an adult letting an old hurt be spoken to a trusted person when it surfaces, and turning to a counsellor for support.

passage:
Eshaan,

It's late, and I'm writing instead of pretending I'm fine, which is new for me.

Today at the mall they had a big banner for Father's Day, and a little girl was choosing a card with her dad. I stood there and started crying. Over a card. It's been twelve years since Baba left us, and I thought I'd sealed that away.

My old way would be to go home, clean the whole kitchen and not think about it. Instead I came home and wrote three pages. Then I cried properly. It was awful, and also, weirdly, lighter after.

I think I'm going to book a session with the counsellor my friend saw. This keeps coming up every June, and I don't want to carry it alone.

Call me this week? I'd like to talk about him with you. You were there too.

Bidisha

qa.q: How long has it been since Baba left?
qa.a: Twelve years.

qa.q: Why did Bidisha write three pages instead of cleaning the kitchen?
qa.a: Bidisha felt the old hurt surface and, rather than shove it down, chose to let the feeling out, which left Bidisha feeling lighter afterwards.

qa.q: Why is booking a counsellor a sensible step for Bidisha?
qa.a: Because the hurt keeps coming back every June, a qualified counsellor can help Bidisha work through it rather than carry it alone.

qa.q: How might Eshaan feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Eshaan may feel moved and close to Bidisha, since Eshaan shared the same loss and is being invited to talk about it.

grounding: Shows an adult writing and crying when an old hurt surfaces instead of pushing it down, and choosing to see a counsellor.

passage: Lokesh, you asked why I skipped the second night of the school reunion. I'll tell you, since you're the one I trust. So: Bidisha, honest version. On the first night, the old gang laughed about how they used to leave me out of the lunch table, as a joke. Everyone laughed. I laughed too. Then I got in the car and sobbed so hard I couldn't drive. I'd told myself for years that it didn't matter. It mattered. Before, I would have gone back the next night and smiled. This time I called you, remember, and just said it out loud, all of it. It hurt more to say it, and then it hurt less. It kept coming back for weeks, though, at odd moments. So I've started seeing a counsellor every other Thursday. It's slow. But it's the first time I've let that year be real.

qa.q: How often does Bidisha see the counsellor?
qa.a: Every other Thursday.

qa.q: Why did Bidisha sob in the car after laughing along?
qa.a: The joke touched an old hurt from being left out at school, which Bidisha had buried, and the feeling came flooding out once alone.

qa.q: What choice helped Bidisha move forward, and why?
qa.a: Calling Lokesh and saying it all aloud, then seeing a counsellor when it kept returning, let the hurt be spoken and supported rather than buried again.

qa.q: How might Lokesh feel being the first one Bidisha called?
qa.a: Lokesh likely feels trusted and caring, and glad to have been there to listen.

grounding: Shows an adult speaking an old hurt aloud to a trusted friend when it surfaces, and turning to a counsellor when it persists.

I've shared an office with Sudha for two years. Last month, after a meeting about layoffs, she went very quiet. The next morning, I saw her eyes were red.

Over tea, she told me the meeting reminded her of when her father lost his job when she was twelve. "I thought I was over it," she said.

She didn't shove it down. That week she wrote in a notebook at lunch, and on Friday she said, "I talked to my cousin Nandini last night and cried for an hour. It helped."

Later she mentioned she'd booked a session with the company counsellor. I don't know everything she felt. But I saw her let the old hurt speak, instead of hiding it.

qa.q: What did the meeting remind Sudha of?
qa.a: When her father lost his job when she was twelve.

qa.q: What does Sudha's crying for an hour with Nandini suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt the old hurt deeply and was relieved to let it out instead of hiding it.

qa.q: What steps did Sudha take when the old hurt surfaced?
qa.a: She wrote in a notebook, talked to Nandini and booked a session with the company counsellor.

qa.a: Nandini probably felt caring and glad Sudha trusted her.

passage:
Jagdish, you think crying makes you weak? Let your Rukmini didi tell you something.

When I was twenty-five, my best friend moved abroad. That same week, I found myself crying over nothing: a song, an old photo, my mother's voice on the phone. I realised it was about more than my friend. It was about my grandmother, who died when I was ten. I never cried for her then.

I could have pushed it down again. Instead I wrote letters to my grandmother, letters I never sent. I talked to my mother about her. When the sadness didn't lift, I saw a counsellor for a few months.

It was hard. But it felt like finally opening a window in a closed room.

qa.q: What did Rukmini write to her grandmother?
qa.a: Letters she never sent.

qa.q: How did young Rukmini feel that week her friend moved abroad?
qa.a: She felt deep sadness that went beyond her friend, as old grief for her grandmother surfaced.

qa.q: What turning point in the story led Rukmini to see a counsellor?
qa.a: When the sadness didn't lift after writing and talking, she chose to see a counsellor.

qa.q: How might Rukmini's mother have felt talking about the grandmother?
qa.a: Her mother probably felt moved and glad to share memories.

grounding: An elder recalls letting old grief be spoken through letters, family talk and a counsellor instead of burying it again.

passage: Akash's manager at the Bengaluru office said, "Is this the best you can do?" and something in Akash went cold. For three days he couldn't shake it. The words were his father's, from the day he failed his board exam. He had never talked about that day. On the third night, his wife Preeti found him sitting in the dark kitchen. Instead of saying "I'm fine", he said, "Can I tell you something from when I was sixteen?" He told her. His voice broke twice. She held his hand. The next week, because the heaviness kept coming back, he booked a session with a counsellor through his office's support line. "I'm tired of carrying it alone," he told Preeti.

qa.q: What did the manager say?

qa.q: Why did the manager's words make Akash go cold?

qa.q: What did Akash do differently this time?

qa.q: What is it like for Preeti when Akash opens up?
qa.a: She is probably moved and relieved to be let in, holding his hand as his voice breaks.

"You left the wedding hall pretty fast, Pranav."
"The speech got to me. The bit about families staying together."
"Want to talk about it?"
"My usual answer is no."
"And today's answer?"
He sat on the steps. "When I was nine, my parents split. I never cried about it. I just got good at school."
"And today it came back."
"Like a wave. I'm twenty-five, Kiran. It's embarrassing."
"It's not. You're feeling something you parked for sixteen years."
"I don't know what to do with it."
"Cry if you need to. Talk to me. And if it keeps knocking, see a counsellor. My sister did, after her own stuff."
He wiped his eyes. "Okay. Starting with the crying, apparently."

qa.q: How old was Pranav when his parents split?
qa.a: Nine.

qa.q: What did Pranav feel during the wedding speech?
qa.a: A wave of old grief about his parents' split, plus embarrassment at feeling it at twenty-five.

qa.q: What did Kiran suggest?
qa.a: Cry if he needs to, talk to Kiran, and see a counsellor if the feeling keeps knocking.

qa.q: How might Kiran feel sitting with Pranav?
qa.a: Kiran seems caring and steady, glad Pranav chose to talk instead of giving the usual no.

grounding: An adult lets an old hurt be spoken and cried over instead of pushing it down, with a counsellor as a next step if it persists.

passage:
Last month, clearing out Nani's old trunk, I found my Class 5 report card, from the year Papa left. The teacher's comment said: "Payal has become very quiet." I sat on the floor and something in my chest cracked open.
My old habit would have been to shut the trunk, put on a podcast and clean the whole flat. This time I let myself cry. Then I wrote two pages about that year in my notebook, messy and unfair and true. That evening I called Gurleen and read one paragraph aloud. She didn't try to fix anything; she just said, "That sounds so lonely."
It still aches sometimes. So I've booked a session with a counsellor for next week, because I'd rather not carry this alone again.

qa.q: What did Payal find in Nani's trunk?
qa.a: The Class 5 report card from the year Papa left.

qa.q: Why did Payal choose to cry instead of shutting the trunk?
qa.a: Payal felt an old, deep sadness and chose to let it be felt rather than bury it again, sensing that pushing it down had never really worked.

qa.q: Which steps helped Payal handle the old hurt?
qa.a: Crying, writing about that year, reading a paragraph aloud to Gurleen, and booking a counsellor because the ache keeps coming back.

qa.q: How might Gurleen feel hearing that paragraph?
qa.a: Gurleen probably feels moved and trusted, and chooses to listen and name the loneliness instead of rushing to fix it.

grounding: An adult lets an old childhood hurt be felt, written down and shared with a trusted person, and books a counsellor when it keeps aching.
